Edge Illusion

GeometryTrianglesCircles
Game: This is an illusion to explore, not a game to win: a triangle or a square seems to appear even though no one draws its sides.
How to play: Change the shape, the number of circles and how much of each circle you see, then try the four drawing modes. Drag the dot on the ruler or focus it and use the arrow keys; press S to switch the colours.

Drag the purple dot on the ruler, or focus it and press the arrow keys. Keys: [ and ] change the number of circles, − and + change the fill, T changes the shape, M the drawing mode, S the colours, X the extra shapes, R resets.

Look for the math

Nothing here changes colour in the middle of the picture. The surprise is what your eyes make of the pieces around it: the classic Kanizsa figure. Here is the page's own claim and exactly what the applet draws.

The claim, word for word

Bogomolny's page says: Do you perceive edgeless triangle (square)? Does this shape appear brighter than the surrounding background? (Compare this to the Simultaneous Contrast Illusion.) The effect is known as a subjective (or illusory ) contour. For a recognizable simlpe shape the brain appears to supply edges. Once edges are used elsewhere the shape becomes less prominent. (The spelling and spacing are the original page's.) A computer can check the drawable part of that: in the plain, fill and paint modes no line joins the corners, and the middle is filled with the same field colour as the outside. It cannot check what you see. "Brighter" is a fact about eyes, not about the paint; this is a subjective contour, not a shaded polygon.

Where the circles sit

Let R = min(width, height) / 3 with Java's integer division, and let the centre be (cx, cy). The triangle puts three corner centres at angles 90° + 120°i on that circle, with its centre lowered by cy / 12; the square puts four at 45° + 90°i with no lowered centre. Every circle centre uses Java's Math.round, and the ruler distance D between the first two centres is truncated to a whole number. With N rings and P percent fill, the applet's step is D · P / 100 / (2N − 1) / 2; ring j has radius round((2N − j − 1) · step). The test compares all of these with a second transcription of the bytecode.

Why the middle looks empty

The rings are drawn first. Then the polygon through the corner centres is filled with the background colour, so the parts of the rings inside it vanish under a patch exactly the same colour as the rest of the field. That is the "edgeless" triangle or square: only the notches facing inward are left. Press Edges and the applet adds pairs of short strokes along the two sides meeting at each corner. Those strokes are the edges that the brain had been supplying, which is why the shape becomes less prominent when they are there. The status line counts them.

Options, defaults and small changes

The live cut-the-knot page still embeds the Java applet with CODE="EdgeIllusion", archive="CTKUtility.zip,EdgeIllusion.zip" and bcolor=ffffff, so no Wayback copy was needed. The applet opens on a triangle with N = 2, P = 50 and Draw plain checked. Its AWT scrollbars are Scrollbar(0, 2, 1, 1, 11) and Scrollbar(0, 50, 5, 0, 105), so usable values are 1..10 and 0..100 — the maximum stops at maximum − visibleAmount. Its foreground is fcolor=000000; here the two roles follow the site's light and dark colour tokens, and Switch colors trades them as the applet does. Paint mode's seven fixed colours are the applet's own palette, brightened a little so they read at night. Extra shapes use the applet's own odd factors, sqrt(3)/2 for the triangle and 1/2 for the square. The logic test checks all 32,320 option combinations at the board size and 1,792 more at four other sizes; no rule was simplified.

Start with the triangle at 2 circles, press Edges to see the missing sides appear, then press Paint and Extra shapes before switching the colours.
